kit/items — item definitions and stack-aware inventories

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Replicated inventory stateDefinitions: the TableSlots and operationsOperations that require the TableWorked example: looting a chestGrid packingInventory invariants and return values

kit/items represents inventories in bags, chests, and pickups. It provides a 4-byte Slot, a definition Table containing names and stack sizes, and deterministic add, take, put, and transfer operations. Use table-free operations inside predicted commands; perform operations that need item definitions in the authority hook that holds the table.

Inventories normally use reliable delta fields mutated through commands. Table-free Slot operations are pure and deterministic and can run inside predicted commands on either lane. Inventory($N) has not been covered by the simulation-descriptor tests; do not put it on the simulation lane without adding that coverage.

Replicated inventory state#

An inventory stores a fixed-size array of 4-byte Slot values in a replicated entity struct:

Odin
Chest :: struct {
	slots: [8]kitems.Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
	...
}

Tag the inventory as replicated state. kit/net then compares slots with its stored copy and sends changes as it does for other fixed-layout fields. When a command predicate rejects a conflicting prediction, the reply includes authority inventory state for correction.

Operations are deterministic and allocation-free. A predicting client and the host produce identical slots when given the same starting state and arguments. Their starting state can differ during contention: two players taking the last item may both predict success. The host processes their commands in arrival order; the second finds the slot empty and rejects. The command pipeline returns the verdict and corrects the rejected prediction.

Every peer registers the same item definitions in ready(), using game constants for IDs. The inventory replicates 4-byte slots containing those IDs and counts; it does not send the definition table.

Definitions: the Table#

Odin
Item_Id :: distinct u16

// The empty-slot marker. Real items start at 1.
ITEM_NONE :: Item_Id(0)

Item_Def :: struct {
	name:      string, // owned by the table
	max_stack: u16, // 1 = unstackable
	shape:     Shape, // grid footprint (packing below); zero = 1x1
}

Table :: struct {
	defs: map[Item_Id]Item_Def,
}

// Declare (or redeclare — safe in ready() every run) an item kind. `shape`
// only matters to packed grids; slot inventories ignore it.
items_register :: proc(t: ^Table, id: Item_Id, name: string, max_stack: u16 = 1, shape := Shape{})

items_def :: proc(t: ^Table, id: Item_Id) -> (Item_Def, bool)

// Display name ("" for empty or unknown items).
items_name :: proc(t: ^Table, id: Item_Id) -> string

table_destroy :: proc(t: ^Table)

Cavecrawl registers its table once in ready() (cavecrawl.odin):

Odin
kitems.items_register(&self.table, GEM, "gem", 99)
kitems.items_register(&self.table, TORCH, "torch", 5)

Slots and operations#

Odin
// One inventory slot: 4 POD bytes. An empty slot must be exactly
// {ITEM_NONE, 0} — every op normalizes on the way out, so slot equality (and
// the replication layer's byte-level diffing) stays meaningful.
Slot :: struct {
	item:  Item_Id,
	count: u16,
}

// Add `count` of `item`: tops up existing stacks first, then fills empty
// slots. Returns how many were actually added (0 = inventory full).
add :: proc(t: ^Table, slots: []Slot, item: Item_Id, count: u16) -> (added: u16)

// Remove up to `count` of `item` from anywhere. Returns how many came out.
remove :: proc(slots: []Slot, item: Item_Id, count: u16) -> (removed: u16)

count_of :: proc(slots: []Slot, item: Item_Id) -> (total: int)

// Take up to `count` out of one specific slot. Returns what came out
// (ITEM_NONE/0 when the slot was empty — callers check `.count > 0`).
take :: proc(slots: []Slot, idx: int, count: u16) -> (taken: Slot)

// Put up to `count` of `item` into one specific slot (empty, or a matching
// stack with room). Returns how many went in.
put :: proc(t: ^Table, slots: []Slot, idx: int, item: Item_Id, count: u16) -> (accepted: u16)

// Move up to `count` from one slot of `from` into `to` (stacking rules apply).
// Any remainder returns to the source slot. Both inventories are updated
// together. Returns how many moved.
transfer :: proc(t: ^Table, from: []Slot, from_idx: int, to: []Slot, count: u16) -> (moved: u16)

// The `slots: [N]Slot gd:"replicate"` field, packaged: embed it (`using inv:
// kitems.Inventory(8)`) and the array replicates like a flat field, while
// inv_add/inv_remove/inv_count/inv_take/inv_put/inv_transfer forward to
// `slots[:]` — growing ops still take the Table, drain/read ops stay command-safe.
Inventory :: struct($N: int) {
	slots: [N]Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
}

Operations that require the Table#

Operations that can grow a stack consult the definitions for max_stack: add, put, and transfer. Operations that only remove or read items do not need the table: take, remove, and count_of.

Use the table-free operations inside a @(gd_command) proc, which sees only its target entity and arguments. Add items with stacking rules in the command hook or host code that has access to the table.

Worked example: looting a chest#

The command removes items without consulting the table and can therefore be predicted. It checks range with the same kit/interact procedure used by the prompt. The example below shows a local scratch-field approach; the current examples/cavecrawl/scripts/chest.odin returns the taken Slot to its generated consequence instead:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
chest_take :: proc(self: ^Chest, slot: i32, px: f32, py: f32) -> bool {
	if !kinter.in_range({px, py, 0}, {self.x, self.y, 0}, REACH) {return false}
	taken := kitems.take(self.slots[:], int(slot), 99) // the whole stack
	if taken.count == 0 {return false}
	self.last_take = taken
	return true
}

Crediting another entity runs only on the host, in a command hook that can access the table. A host.odin handler can apply it as follows:

Odin
cave_credit :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby, player: knet.Player_Id, chest: ^Chest) {
	av, has := self.avatar_of[player]
	if !has {return}
	sp := self.spelunkers[av]
	credited := kitems.add(&self.table, sp.bag[:], chest.last_take.item, chest.last_take.count)
	if leftover := chest.last_take.count - credited; leftover > 0 {
		_ = kitems.add(&self.table, chest.slots[:], chest.last_take.item, leftover)
	}
}

In this example, last_take is an unreplicated scratch field that carries the removed Slot to the hook. kit/ui's inv_refresh renders the bag from the same slots and table.

Grid packing#

For inventories with spatial footprints, such as 2x3 rifles or 3x3 crates, packing.odin provides a board represented by a fixed array of 10-byte Packed_Entry values inside a replicated struct. Pass board dimensions as game constants to its operations.

Odin
Stash :: struct {
	grid: [12]kitems.Packed_Entry `gd:"replicate"`,
}

// ready(), every peer:
items_register(&table, RIFLE, "rifle", shape = kitems.shape_of("XXX"))
items_register(&table, BOOT, "boot", shape = kitems.shape_of("X.", "X.", "XX"))

Shapes use a solid-cell mask up to 4x4; shape_of builds it from row strings. Each entry stores its shape, allowing pack_move, pack_remove, pack_at, and pack_fits to run without a table inside commands. A drag-to-rearrange command can use one predicted pack_move. Operations that add placements run in host code or hooks with the table: pack_place takes a looked-up shape, while pack_add stacks items and finds space for new entries.

pack_find_spot scans in row-major order, so a prediction and the host derive the same placement anchor from the same grid bytes. If two players predict a move into the same corner, the host processes them in arrival order and rejects the conflicting move. The rejected prediction then reverts.

Inventory invariants and return values#

  • Keep command-side operations deterministic: no table, allocation, or clocks. Re-execution on the host must produce the same slots from the same state and arguments.
  • An empty slot is exactly {ITEM_NONE, 0}; every op normalizes on the way out. Don't hand-write slots that break this: replication diffs bytes.
  • Unknown (unregistered) items get max_stack = 1: they refuse to stack rather than merge blindly.
  • items_register asserts on id 0 (the empty-slot marker), and re-registration is safe: call it in ready() every run, on every peer, with the same constants.
  • Check returned counts. add may credit fewer items than requested when the inventory is full. Handle the remainder, as cave_credit does by returning it to the chest.
